claim: The human mitotic spindle is made of microtubules nucleated at centrosomes, at kinetochores, and from pre-existing microtubules by the augmin complex.
source: The human mitotic spindle is made of microtubules nucleated at centrosomes, at kinetochores, and from pre-existing microtubules by the augmin complex.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition and nucleation mechanisms of the human mitotic spindle, drawing from established scientific knowledge about spindle assembly.

claim: Augmin is vital for the formation of uniformly arranged parallel units consisting of sister kinetochore fibers connected by a bridging fiber.
source: Here, we use superresolution microscopy to analyze the previously indistinguishable microtubule arrangements within the crowded metaphase plate area and demonstrate that augmin is vital for the formation of uniformly arranged parallel units consisting of sister kinetochore fibers connected by a bridging fiber.
evidence: The claim is supported by superresolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript showing microtubule arrangements in control and augmin-depleted cells.

claim: Augmin-nucleated bridging fibers prevent merotelic attachments by creating a nearly parallel and highly bundled microtubule arrangement unfavorable for creating additional attachments.
source: Whereas augmin-nucleated bridging fibers prevent merotelic attachments by creating a nearly parallel and highly bundled microtubule arrangement unfavorable for creating additional attachments, augmin-nucleated k-fibers produce robust force required to resolve errors during anaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of merotelic attachments in augmin-depleted cells and analysis of kinetochore orientation and tension.

claim: Augmin-nucleated k-fibers produce robust force required to resolve errors during anaphase.
source: Whereas augmin-nucleated bridging fibers prevent merotelic attachments by creating a nearly parallel and highly bundled microtubule arrangement unfavorable for creating additional attachments, augmin-nucleated k-fibers produce robust force required to resolve errors during anaphase.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that misaligned chromosomes are more likely to missegregate in augmin-depleted cells and that anaphase A speed is reduced.

claim: STED microscopy revealed that bridging fibers were impaired twice as much as k-fibers following augmin depletion.
source: STED microscopy revealed that bridging fibers were impaired twice as much as k-fibers following augmin depletion.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of tubulin signal intensity in bridging fibers and k-fibers using STED microscopy.

claim: The complete absence of bridging fibers from a significant portion of kinetochore pairs, especially in the inner part of the spindle, resulted in the specific reduction of the interkinetochore distance.
source: The complete absence of bridging fibers from a significant portion of kinetochore pairs, especially in the inner part of the spindle, resulted in the specific reduction of the interkinetochore distance.
evidence: This is supported by measurements showing that kinetochore pairs without bridging fibers have reduced interkinetochore distance, particularly in the inner spindle region.

claim: The mitotic spindle consists of three major classes of microtubules: kinetochore microtubules that form kinetochore fibers (k-fibers) connecting chromosomes to the spindle pole through kinetochores, midplane-crossing microtubules that form antiparallel arrays in the central part of the spindle, and astral microtubules that extend from the spindle poles towards the cell cortex.
source: It consists of three major classes of microtubules: kinetochore microtubules that form kinetochore fibers (k-fibers) connecting chromosomes to the spindle pole through kinetochores, midplane-crossing microtubules that form antiparallel arrays in the central part of the spindle, and astral microtubules that extend from the spindle poles towards the cell cortex (McIntosh, 2016; O'Toole et al., 2020; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature describing spindle architecture.

claim: During metaphase and early anaphase, the majority of midplane-crossing microtubule bundles are laterally attached to a pair of sister k-fibers resembling a bridge between them, which is why they are called bridging fibers.
source: During metaphase and early anaphase, the majority of midplane-crossing microtubule bundles are laterally attached to a pair of sister k-fibers resembling a bridge between them, which is why they are called bridging fibers (Kajtez et al., 2016; Vukušić et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work that characterized bridging fibers.

claim: Bridging fibers balance the tension between sister kinetochores and maintain the curved shape of the metaphase spindle.
source: These fibers balance the tension between sister kinetochores and maintain the curved shape of the metaphase spindle (Kajtez et al., 2016; Polak et al., 2017; Tolić and Pavin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on bridging fiber function.

claim: Spindle microtubules in human somatic cells are generated by several nucleation mechanisms, including centrosome-dependent and augmin-dependent nucleation.
source: Spindle microtubules in human somatic cells are generated by several nucleation mechanisms, including centrosome-dependent and augmin-dependent nucleation (Kirschner and Mitchison, 1986; Pavin and Tolić, 2016; Petry, 2016; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017; Wu et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2008), with an addition of chromatin- and kinetochore-dependent nucleation as a third mechanism that contributes to the directional formation of k-fibers (Maiato et al., 2004; Sikirzhytski et al., 2018; Tulu et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature on microtubule nucleation mechanisms.

claim: Augmin is an eight-subunit protein complex that serves as a recruiter of the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) required for microtubule nucleation.
source: However, numerous studies revealed that a significant number of microtubules also arise from pre-existing microtubules, through augmin, an eight-subunit protein complex that serves as a recruiter of the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) required for microtubule nucleation (David et al., 2019; Goshima et al., 2008; Kamasaki et al., 2013; Lawo et al., 2009; Song et al., 2018; Uehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies characterizing augmin structure and function.

claim: Augmin-nucleated microtubules grow at an angle of 0-30° relative to the pre-existing microtubule.
source: Augmin-nucleated microtubules grow at an angle of 0-30o relative to the pre-existing microtubule (Kamasaki et al., 2013; Petry et al., 2013; Verma and Maresca, 2019) and show a directional bias towards kinetochores, resulting in the preserved polarity of the spindle once the initial kinetochore-microtubule attachments form (David et al., 2019; Kamasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies measuring the angle of augmin-nucleated microtubule growth.

claim: Augmin-nucleated microtubules show a directional bias towards kinetochores, resulting in the preserved polarity of the spindle once the initial kinetochore-microtubule attachments form.
source: Augmin-nucleated microtubules grow at an angle of 0-30o relative to the pre-existing microtubule (Kamasaki et al., 2013; Petry et al., 2013; Verma and Maresca, 2019) and show a directional bias towards kinetochores, resulting in the preserved polarity of the spindle once the initial kinetochore-microtubule attachments form (David et al., 2019; Kamasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing directional growth of augmin-nucleated microtubules.

claim: Depletion of augmin complex results in impairment of microtubule bundles within the spindle accompanied by the formation of long, curved bundles on the spindle periphery, loss of spindle bipolarity, shorter interkinetochore distance, chromosome misalignment, mitotic delays, and a higher incidence of aneuploidy and cytokinesis failure.
source: Depletion of augmin complex in different cell types results in impairment of microtubule bundles within the spindle accompanied by the formation of long, curved bundles on the spindle periphery, loss of spindle bipolarity, shorter interkinetochore distance, chromosome misalignment, mitotic delays, and a higher incidence of aneuploidy and cytokinesis failure (Almeida et al., 2022; Hayward et al., 2014; Uehara and Goshima, 2010; Uehara et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on augmin depletion phenotypes.

claim: HAUS6 and HAUS8 are two directly interacting subunits of the augmin complex that have been extensively studied because of their ability to interact with a γ-TuRC adapter protein NEDD1 and pre-existing microtubules, respectively.
source: Of the eight subunits in the complex, the two directly interacting subunits HAUS6 (hDgt6/FAM29A) and HAUS8 (hDgt4/Hice1) have been extensively studied because of their ability to interact with a γ-TuRC adapter protein NEDD1 and pre-existing microtubules, respectively (Song et al., 2018; Uehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing HAUS6 and HAUS8 interactions.

claim: Ends of midplane-crossing microtubules interact with the wall of kinetochore microtubules.
source: Recent electron tomography work on spindles in human cells showed that ends of midplane-crossing microtubules interact with the wall of kinetochore microtubules (O'Toole et al., 2020), indicating that augmin-dependent nucleation might play an important role in their formation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electron tomography study.

claim: Augmin depletion has been linked to higher incidence of segregation errors.
source: Augmin depletion has previously been linked to higher incidence of segregation errors (Wu et al., 2008) and the appearance of lagging chromosomes (Almeida et al., 2022; Viais et al., 2021), which were connected to impaired brain development in a recent study (Viais et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on augmin depletion and segregation errors.

claim: Lagging chromosomes following augmin depletion were connected to impaired brain development.
source: Augmin depletion has previously been linked to higher incidence of segregation errors (Wu et al., 2008) and the appearance of lagging chromosomes (Almeida et al., 2022; Viais et al., 2021), which were connected to impaired brain development in a recent study (Viais et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study linking augmin depletion to brain development defects.

claim: Homozygous loss of HAUS6 subunit of the augmin complex was seen in several cancer types, such as sarcomas, pancreatic adenocarcinomas, gliomas, and glioblastomas.
source: Homozygous loss of HAUS6 subunit of the augmin complex was also seen in several cancer types, such as sarcomas, pancreatic adenocarcinomas, gliomas, and glioblastomas (ICGC/TCGA, 2020, retrieved by using cBioPortal Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cancer genomics databases and cBioPortal.

claim: In control cells, the vast majority of midplane-crossing microtubule bundles laterally attached to a pair of sister k-fibers and formed a bridging fiber between them.
source: In control cells, the vast majority of midplane-crossing microtubule bundles laterally attached to a pair of sister k-fibers and formed a bridging fiber between them, consistent with previous findings (Kajtez et al., 2016; Vukušić et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images shown in Figure 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Bridging fibers in control cells were nearly-parallel with respect to one another and the spindle axis.
source: These bridging fibers were nearly-parallel with respect to one another and the spindle axis.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: A small portion of midplane-crossing microtubules formed a secondary connection between a k-fiber on one side and a non-sister k-fiber on the other side.
source: Additionally, a small portion of midplane-crossing microtubules formed a secondary connection between a k-fiber on one side and a non-sister k-fiber on the other side (O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electron tomography study.

claim: After HAUS6 or HAUS8 depletion, midplane-crossing microtubules extended at a variety of angles, and were wavy and disordered, particularly in the inner part of the spindle close to the pole-to-pole axis.
source: In comparison with untreated cells, midplane-crossing microtubules after HAUS6 or HAUS8 depletion extended at a variety of angles, and were wavy and disordered, particularly in the inner part of the spindle close to the pole-to-pole axis.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: Following HAUS6 or HAUS8 depletion, midplane-crossing microtubules less often formed bridging fibers that connect to sister k-fibers.
source: Strikingly, midplane-crossing microtubules less often formed bridging fibers that connect to sister k-fibers in cells depleted of HAUS6 or HAUS8.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: After augmin depletion, midplane-crossing microtubules formed more complex arrangements, primarily consisting of one or more connections between various k-fibers within the metaphase spindle.
source: Instead, they formed more complex arrangements, primarily consisting of one or more connections between various k-fibers within the metaphase spindle.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: K-fibers following augmin depletion, even though often missing a bridge between them, appeared relatively similar to those in control cells.
source: This was contrary to k-fibers which, even though often missing a bridge between them, appeared relatively similar to those in control cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion resulted in a total of 5.7±0.8 segregation errors per cell, compared to 1.5±0.2 in Mad2 depletion alone.
source: The treatment with Mad2 siRNA resulted in a total of 1.5±0.2 segregation errors per cell (all data are given as mean ± SEM). However, the effect was significantly more severe when Mad2 was codepleted with HAUS6, resulting in a total of 5.7±0.8 segregation errors per cell (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of misaligned kinetochore pairs per cell was similar in both Mad2 depletion and Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion.
source: Tracking of sister kinetochores in live-cell videos revealed that the number of misaligned kinetochore pairs per cell was similar in both Mad2 depletion and Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion (Figure 2B), which is why we presume they appeared due to Mad2 depletion independently of HAUS6 depletion.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Misaligned kinetochore pairs were much more likely to missegregate in cells without HAUS6, where 80 ± 9% of kinetochore pairs jointly segregated into the same cell, compared to only 20 ± 13% in control cells.
source: Nevertheless, they were much more likely to missegregate in cells without HAUS6, where 80 ± 9% of kinetochore pairs jointly segregated into the same cell, compared to only 20 ± 13% in control cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion, there were 2.6±0.4 lagging kinetochores per cell, and 45 ± 6% of all lagging kinetochores ultimately missegregated.
source: Interestingly, lagging kinetochores were both more frequent and more likely to missegregate in cells with Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion, in which there were 2.6±0.4 lagging kinetochores per cell, and 45 ± 6% of all lagging kinetochores ultimately missegregated.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Mad2 depletion, there were only 0.8±0.2 lagging kinetochore pairs per cell, and 77 ± 8% of them segregated correctly.
source: In contrast, there were only 0.8±0.2 lagging kinetochore pairs per cell in Mad2 depletion, and 77 ± 8% of them segregated correctly (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both poleward movement of kinetochores during anaphase A and spindle elongation during anaphase B were reduced following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Uehara et al., 2009), both poleward movement of kinetochores during anaphase A and spindle elongation during anaphase B were reduced following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F and a citation to previous work.

claim: The kinetochore closer to the proximal pole approached the proximal pole during anaphase A both after Mad2 depletion and Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion.
source: The kinetochore closer to the proximal pole approached the proximal pole during anaphase A both after Mad2 depletion and Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion, thereby moving towards the pole to which it should segregate in both cases (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Mad2-depleted cells, the kinetochore further away from the proximal pole typically moved towards the distal pole and accurately segregated as a 'lazy' kinetochore.
source: However, the kinetochore further away from the proximal pole usually remained stagnant for a short period of time, and afterwards typically moved towards the distal pole and accurately segregated as a 'lazy' kinetochore (Sen et al., 2021) in Mad2-depleted cells.
evidence: This is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to previous work on lazy kinetochores.

claim: In Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells, the kinetochore further away from the proximal pole typically moved away from the pole to which it should segregate, thereby missegregating.
source: In contrast, the kinetochore further away from the proximal pole experienced a short stagnation period and then typically moved away from the pole to which it should segregate, thereby missegregating in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-H).
evidence: This is supported by tracking data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: The interkinetochore distance of both correctly and incorrectly segregating misaligned kinetochore pairs in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells was similar.
source: As the interkinetochore distance of both correctly and incorrectly segregating misaligned kinetochore pairs in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells was similar (Figure 2E), the absence of biorientation is unlikely to be the cause of missegregation for these kinetochores.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Missegregation of misaligned kinetochores in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells likely occurs due to k-fibers with fewer microtubules creating insufficient force to move the kinetochore towards the distal pole.
source: Instead, missegregation likely occurs due to k-fibers with fewer microtubules (Almeida et al., 2022; Uehara et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2008) creating insufficient force to move the kinetochore towards the distal pole (Dudka et al., 2018), against the movement of neighboring kinetochores and the corresponding chromosome mass which travel towards the proximal pole (Figure 2A, Video 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on data from the current study and citations to previous work on k-fiber function.

claim: In Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells, 19 ± 5% of all lagging kinetochore pairs were situated in the inner part of the spindle just before anaphase onset.
source: Remarkably, in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells, 19 ± 5% of all lagging kinetochore pairs were situated in the inner part of the spindle just before anaphase onset (Figure 2F), where disordered midplane-crossing microtubules most frequently appeared.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In Mad2-depleted cells, all lagging kinetochore pairs were situated in the outer half of the spindle just before anaphase onset.
source: In Mad2-depleted cells, all lagging kinetochore pairs were situated in the outer half of the spindle just before anaphase onset.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The lagging kinetochore pairs in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells had an interkinetochore distance of 0.89±0.03 µm, which was significantly smaller than the interkinetochore distance of 0.98±0.02 µm measured in error-free kinetochore pairs.
source: The lagging kinetochore pairs in Mad2/HAUS6-codepleted cells had an interkinetochore distance of 0.89±0.03 µm, which was significantly smaller than the interkinetochore distance of 0.98±0.02 µm measured in error-free kinetochore pairs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Lagging kinetochore pairs in Mad2-depleted cells had an interkinetochore distance of 1.10±0.05 µm, similar to the interkinetochore distance of 1.05±0.02 µm measured in error-free kinetochore pairs.
source: This was not the case for lagging kinetochore pairs in Mad2-depleted cells which had an interkinetochore distance of 1.10±0.05 µm, similar to the interkinetochore distance of 1.05±0.02 µm measured in error-free kinetochore pairs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion, lagging kinetochore pairs had a tilt of 19.7±1.6° and error-free kinetochore pairs had a tilt of 10.9±0.8°.
source: As for the interkinetochore distance following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion, lagging kinetochore pairs were different from error-free kinetochore pairs, the tilt of which was 19.7±1.6° and 10.9±0.8°, respectively (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In Mad2-depleted cells, there was no difference in tilt between lagging kinetochore pairs (8.2±1.5°) and error-free kinetochore pairs (8.9±0.6°).
source: In contrast, in Mad2-depleted cells with preserved spindle geometry there was no difference between lagging kinetochore pairs with the tilt of 8.2±1.5° and error-free kinetochore pairs with the tilt of 8.9±0.6°, which was also similar to the tilt of 10.9±0.8° measured for error-free kinetochore pairs following Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The tilt of kinetochores inversely correlated with the interkinetochore distance in augmin depletion, but not in control cells.
source: The tilt of kinetochores inversely correlated with the interkinetochore distance in augmin depletion, but not in control cells (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Merotelic attachments were found in HAUS6-depleted cells imaged using STED microscopy, with most kinetochores forming an attachment with the microtubule from the opposite side of the mitotic spindle, while missing a proper bridging fiber.
source: Indeed, we found merotelic attachments in HAUS6-depleted cells imaged using STED microscopy, with most kinetochores forming an attachment with the microtubule from the opposite side of the mitotic spindle, while missing a proper bridging fiber (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Cold treatment combined with STED microscopy confirmed the true merotelic nature of the observed attachments by removing midplane-crossing microtubules and preserving only kinetochore microtubules.
source: To further test the nature of the observed attachments, we combined STED microscopy with cold treatment to remove midplane-crossing microtubules and preserve only kinetochore microtubules (DeLuca et al., 2006; Sacristan et al., 2018; Silkworth et al., 2012), which allowed us to confirm their true merotelic nature (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy images after cold treatment shown in Figure 2K and citations to previous methods.

claim: A larger percentage of lagging kinetochore pairs ends up missegregating in Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion than in Mad2 depletion.
source: Interestingly, our live-cell imaging experiments reveal that augmin is required not only to prevent the formation of merotelic attachments in metaphase, but also to resolve them in anaphase, as a larger percentage of lagging kinetochore pairs ends up missegregating in Mad2/HAUS6 codepletion than in Mad2 depletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HAUS6 depletion resulted in 68 ± 8% reduction of the bridging fiber signal intensity and 24 ± 6% reduction of the k-fiber signal intensity.
source: Quantification of STED images further revealed that HAUS6 depletion resulted in 68 ± 8% reduction of the bridging fiber signal intensity and 24 ± 6% reduction of the k-fiber signal intensity, with similar results obtained by HAUS8 depletion (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from STED images shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: K-fibers in RPE1 cells consist of 12.6 ± 1.7 microtubules.
source: Electron tomography of spindles in RPE1 cells showed that k-fibers consist of nk = 12.6 ± 1.7 microtubules (O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electron tomography study.

claim: Bridging fibers in untreated RPE1 cells consist of 3.8 ± 0.4 microtubules.
source: Thus, the bridging fiber consists of nb = Ib × nk ⁄ Ik = 3.8 ± 0.4 microtubules (for the explanation of Ib and Ik calculations, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is calculated from intensity measurements and the known number of microtubules in k-fibers.

claim: Astral microtubules consist of 1.0 ± 0.1 microtubules.
source: Indeed, using the number of microtubules in the k-fiber, our measurement of astral microtubule intensities showed that the astral microtubules consist of na = 1.0 ± 0.1 microtubules (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is calculated from intensity measurements and serves as a validation of the method.

claim: HAUS6 depletion resulted in a 37 ± 5% reduction of k-fibers in spindles exposed to cold treatment.
source: HAUS6 depletion resulted in a 37 ± 5% reduction of the k-fibers (Figure 3G), which is consistent with a previous study (Zhu et al., 2008) and comparable to values under non-cold conditions.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from STED images after cold treatment shown in Figure 3G and a citation to previous work.

claim: After HAUS6 depletion, bridging fibers consist of 1.2±0.7 microtubules and k-fibers of 9.6±1.5 microtubules, which are interpreted as microtubules nucleated in an augmin-independent manner.
source: Based on the measurements under non-cold conditions, we estimate that after HAUS6 depletion bridging fibers consist of 1.2±0.7 microtubules and k-fibers of 9.6±1.5 microtubules, which we interpret as microtubules nucleated in an augmin-independent manner.
evidence: This is calculated from intensity measurements after augmin depletion.

claim: 2.6±0.7 microtubules in the bridging fiber and 3.0±0.9 microtubules in the k-fiber are nucleated in an augmin-dependent manner.
source: Thus, 2.6±0.7 microtubules in the bridging fiber and 3.0±0.9 microtubules in the k-fiber are nucleated in an augmin-dependent manner.
evidence: This is calculated by subtracting augmin-independent microtubules from the total number in control cells.

claim: 41 ± 4% of all kinetochore pairs in HAUS6-depleted cells had no detectable bridging fibers.
source: Remarkably, 41 ± 4% of all kinetochore pairs in HAUS6-depleted cells had no detectable bridging fibers, defined as those with the tubulin signal below the background signal (see Materials and methods), and consistent with results obtained using visual inspection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of STED images shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In the inner part of the spindle after augmin depletion, 50 ± 5% of all kinetochore pairs had undetectable bridging fibers, compared to only 27 ± 5% in the outer part.
source: The majority of kinetochore pairs without bridging fibers were located in the inner part of the mitotic spindle, where as much as 50 ± 5% of all kinetochore pairs had undetectable bridging fibers after augmin depletion, compared to only 27 ± 5% in the outer part (Figure 3H), thus pointing to an irregular and more complex spatial distribution of bridging fibers in the inner part of the spindles following augmin depletion.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of STED images shown in Figure 3H.

claim: K-fibers without bridging fibers in augmin-depleted cells had a significantly larger radius of curvature than any of the other bundle types in augmin-depleted or control cells.
source: Whereas the bundles without kinetochores in HAUS6 siRNA-treated cells had a significantly longer contour when compared to all other bundle types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J), k-fibers without bridging fibers in augmin-depleted cells had a significantly larger radius of curvature than any of the other bundle types in augmin-depleted or control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of bundle shape shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Poleward flux in U2OS cells was significantly reduced following augmin depletion.
source: In addition to spindle architecture, compromised microtubule nucleation following augmin depletion also affected spindle dynamics, as poleward flux in U2OS cells stably expressing CENP-A-GFP, mCherry-tubulin and photoactivatable-GFP-α-tubulin was significantly reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L-M), in agreement with findings in Indian Muntjac cells (Almeida et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L-M and a citation to previous work.

claim: Both k-fibers and the remaining bridging fibers were significantly slowed down in poleward flux after augmin depletion.
source: Recent speckle microscopy experiments in RPE1 cells, which were able to separate the effect of augmin on poleward flux of bridging and k-fibers, revealed that both k-fibers and the remaining bridging fibers were significantly slowed down (Risteski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study using speckle microscopy.

claim: Bridging fibers fluxed faster than k-fibers in control and augmin-depleted cells.
source: Bridging fibers fluxed faster than k-fibers in control and augmin-depleted cells (Risteski et al., 2022), supporting the model in which poleward flux is largely driven by sliding apart of antiparallel microtubules (Brust-Mascher et al., 2009; Mitchison, 2005; Miyamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent and previous studies on poleward flux mechanisms.

claim: PRC1 depletion does not affect the flux even though it reduces bridging fibers.
source: In contrast, PRC1 depletion does not affect the flux (Risteski et al., 2022; Steblyanko et al., 2020) even though it reduces bridging fibers (Kajtez et al., 2016; Polak et al., 2017), possibly because the remaining bridging microtubules are generated away from the poles via augmin and can thus flux freely.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC1 depletion effects.

claim: The signal intensity of PRC1-GFP bundles in RPE1 cells was reduced by 55 ± 4% following augmin depletion.
source: The signal intensity of PRC1-GFP bundles in RPE1 cells was reduced by 55 ± 4% following augmin depletion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of PRC1-labeled overlap bundles measured in an end-on view of spindles was almost halved; from 28±1 to 16±1 distinct bundles in control and HAUS6-depleted RPE1 cells, respectively.
source: Consistently, the number of PRC1-labeled overlap bundles measured in an end-on view of spindles was almost halved; from 28±1–16±1 distinct bundles in control and HAUS6-depleted RPE1 cells, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Augmin-depleted cells showed a specific barrel-like distribution of the PRC1-GFP labeled bundles, with more overlap bundles being present around the perimeter of the spindle and fewer in the central part.
source: The augmin-depleted cells showed a specific barrel-like distribution of the PRC1-GFP labeled bundles, with more overlap bundles being present around the perimeter of the spindle and fewer in the central part (Figure 4A 'end-on view' and 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-I).
evidence: This is supported by end-on view images and intensity profiles shown in Figure 4.

claim: DNA was uniformly distributed throughout the spindle cross-section, both in augmin-depleted and control cells.
source: However, DNA was uniformly distributed throughout the spindle cross-section, both in augmin-depleted and control cells (Figure 4A 'end-on view').
evidence: This is supported by end-on view images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Kinetochores and tubulin signal were uniformly distributed over the spindle cross-section in both control and augmin-depleted cells.
source: In agreement with this result, kinetochores and tubulin signal were also found uniformly distributed over the spindle cross-section (Figure 4A 'end-on view' of RPE1 cells).
evidence: This is supported by end-on view images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The spindles in RPE1 cells shortened following augmin depletion, while those in HeLa cells were longer.
source: While the spindles in RPE1 cells shortened following augmin depletion, those in HeLa cells were longer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), consistent with previous observations on Drosophila S2 cells and Xenopus egg extracts (Goshima et al., 2007; Petry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J and citations to previous work.

claim: The relative length of overlaps with respect to spindle length increased in RPE1 cells from 48±1% to 57 ± 2% following augmin depletion.
source: When both spindle length and overlap length were taken into account, the relative length of overlaps with respect to spindle length increased in RPE1 cells from 48±1%–57 ± 2% following augmin depletion (Figure 4F), comparable to the increase in HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L-M).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The interkinetochore distance was smaller in the inner part of the spindle in augmin-depleted cells.
source: However, we noticed that the interkinetochore distance was smaller in the inner part of the spindle in augmin-depleted cells (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), where bridging fibers were most severely impaired (Figures 3H and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Control cells showed no difference in interkinetochore distance between the inner and the outer part of the spindle.
source: This was not the case in control cells, which showed no difference in interkinetochore distance between the inner and the outer part of the spindle (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Kinetochore pairs without bridging fibers had a significantly smaller interkinetochore distance than kinetochore pairs with bridging fibers.
source: Remarkably, kinetochore pairs without bridging fibers had a significantly smaller interkinetochore distance than kinetochore pairs with bridging fibers (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kinetochore pairs that lacked a bridging fiber typically had thinner k-fibers than those with a bridging fiber in augmin-depleted cells.
source: Although this result suggests a role of bridging fibers in regulating interkinetochore distance, this effect may be indirect and arise due to k-fibers, askinetochore pairs that lacked a bridging fiber typically had thinner k-fibers than those with a bridging fiber in augmin-depleted cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The interkinetochore distance correlated both with bridging and k-fiber intensity after augmin depletion, but the correlation with bridging fiber intensity was stronger.
source: First, we found that although the interkinetochore distance correlated both with bridging and k-fiber intensity after augmin depletion, the correlation with bridging fiber intensity was stronger (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Such correlations between interkinetochore distance and fiber intensity were absent in control cells.
source: Such correlations were absent in control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: The interkinetochore distance did not correlate with k-fiber intensity within groups of kinetochore pairs with or without bridging fibers in augmin-depleted cells.
source: To explore a specific contribution of k-fibers to the interkinetochore tension, we divided the kinetochore pairs in augmin-depleted cells into two subsets, those with and without bridging fibers, and found that the interkinetochore distance did not correlate with k-fiber intensity within each group (Figure 5F), which argues against the k-fiber intensity as a sole determinant of interkinetochore tension.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When kinetochore pairs with similar k-fiber intensity values were compared, the interkinetochore distance was larger in the subset with bridging fibers than without.
source: Finally, to examine a specific contribution of bridging fibers, we identified two subsets of kinetochore pairs with similar k-fiber intensity values, one of which had bridging fibers and the other which did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We found that the interkinetochore distance was larger in the subset with bridging fibers than without (Figure 5G), indicating a specific effect of bridging fibers on interkinetochore tension.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Augmin has a significant role in regulating interkinetochore tension through the nucleation of bridging microtubules.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that augmin has a significant role in regulating interkinetochore tension through the nucleation of bridging microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bridging fiber forms by augmin-based nucleation of microtubules along the existing microtubules.
source: In this paper, we propose a model of the metaphase spindle in which the bridging fiber, which laterally connects sister k-fibers, forms by augmin-based nucleation of microtubules along the existing microtubules.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The newly nucleated microtubules in the bridging fiber create an antiparallel overlap in which the microtubules slide apart, generating a pushing force that the bridging fiber exerts on its k-fibers.
source: The newly nucleated microtubules in the bridging fiber create an antiparallel overlap in which the microtubules slide apart, generating a pushing force that the bridging fiber exerts on its k-fibers.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental findings and previous knowledge of microtubule sliding.

claim: The bridging fiber works together with k-fibers to produce tension and maintain the appropriate orientation of sister kinetochores parallel to the spindle axis, thereby preventing merotelic attachments and ensuring mitotic fidelity.
source: In doing so, the bridging fiber works together with k-fibers to produce tension and maintain the appropriate orientation of sister kinetochores parallel to the spindle axis, thereby preventing merotelic attachments and ensuring mitotic fidelity (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: The depletion of the augmin complex by silencing the HAUS6 or HAUS8 subunits causes severe thinning of bridging fibers in metaphase spindles.
source: Our work shows that the depletion of the augmin complex by silencing the HAUS6 or HAUS8 subunits causes severe thinning of bridging fibers in metaphase spindles, combined with the appearance of wavy and disordered midplane-crossing microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: K-fibers are largely nucleated in an augmin-independent manner, at the centrosome or kinetochores and chromosomes.
source: K-fibers were also thinner, though to a lesser extent, indicating that they are largely nucleated in an augmin-independent manner, at the centrosome or kinetochores and chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing less severe reduction of k-fibers compared to bridging fibers after augmin depletion.

claim: Most midplane-crossing microtubules start at different points along the k-fiber.
source: In contrast, most midplane-crossing microtubules, which likely correspond to bridging fibers, start at different points along the k-fiber (Mastronarde et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electron microscopy study.

claim: Microtubule minus ends are found along the k-fiber, less than 50 nm from the k-fiber wall and at a distance 2–4 µm from the pole in RPE1 cells.
source: Electron tomography of spindles in RPE1 cells confirmed this result by showing that microtubule minus ends are found along the k-fiber, less than 50 nm from the k-fiber wall and at a distance 2–4 µm from the pole (O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an electron tomography study.

claim: The same number of microtubules in bridging and k-fibers was nucleated by augmin.
source: As we found that the same number of microtubules in bridging and k-fibers was nucleated by augmin, we propose that the existing microtubules orient the growth of augmin-nucleated microtubules (David et al., 2019; Kamasaki et al., 2013), which later become kinetochore microtubules if their plus end binds to the kinetochore or bridging microtubules if they grow past the kinetochore and interact with the bridging or kinetochore microtubules on the other side.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the quantitative data and citations to previous work on microtubule growth directionality.

claim: Augmin-mediated nucleation becomes the predominant pathway of bridging fiber nucleation because there are fewer microtubules in the bridging fiber to begin with.
source: However, as there are less microtubules in the bridging fiber to begin with, augmin-mediated nucleation becomes the predominant pathway of their nucleation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative data showing the proportion of augmin-nucleated microtubules in bridging fibers versus k-fibers.

claim: Treatment of cells with a microtubule-destabilizing agent that results in thinner k-fibers causes a reduction of the interkinetochore tension.
source: Treatment of cells with a microtubule-destabilizing agent that results in thinner k-fibers causes a reduction of the interkinetochore tension (Dudka et al., 2018), supporting the former possibility.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A similar effect on the interkinetochore tension was observed upon perturbation of the bridging fiber by removing the microtubule crosslinker PRC1.
source: However, a similar effect on the interkinetochore tension was observed upon perturbation of the bridging fiber by removing the microtubule crosslinker PRC1 (Jagrić et al., 2021; Kajtez et al., 2016; Polak et al., 2017), in agreement with the latter possibility.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC1 depletion.

claim: Augmin-depleted cells with characteristically compromised bridging fibers have extensive mitotic delays.
source: Considering the importance of the interkinetochore tension for the accuracy of cell division (Lampson and Grishchuk, 2017), the maintenance of tension by the bridging fiber might represent an important mechanism for silencing of the spindle assembly checkpoint (Musacchio and Salmon, 2007; Nicklas et al., 1995), supported by the fact augmin-depleted cells with characteristically compromised bridging fibers have extensive mitotic delays (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on checkpoint function and augmin depletion phenotypes.

claim: Proteins involved in bridging fiber nucleation and crosslinking, including HAUS6, HAUS8, and PRC1 have all been linked to various types of cancer.
source: As proteins involved in bridging fiber nucleation and crosslinking, including HAUS6, HAUS8, and PRC1 have all been linked to various types of cancer (ICGC/TCGA, 2020, retrieved by using cBioPortal Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013), it is plausible that impairment of bridging fibers also leads to such increase in lagging chromosomes and contributes to aneuploidy in cancers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to cancer genomics databases and is presented as a plausible speculation.

claim: Lagging chromosomes that appeared following augmin depletion had a reduced interkinetochore distance, which was consistent with previous findings on lazy chromosomes.
source: Indeed, once the checkpoint was weakened, lagging chromosomes that appeared following augmin depletion had a reduced interkinetochore distance, which was consistent with previous findings on lazy chromosomes (Sen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by data from the current study and a citation to previous work.

claim: Bridging fibers may serve as tracks that guide Aurora B within the Chromosome Passenger Complex towards the kinetochores to correct the errors.
source: Moreover, erroneous attachments might be less likely to undergo error correction in augmin-depleted cells, as bridging fibers may serve as tracks that guide Aurora B within the Chromosome Passenger Complex towards the kinetochores to correct the errors (Matković et al., 2022 Preprint).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a preprint study.
